source.title: The Marketplace of Medina
source.summary: How the Prophet established the first regulated Islamic marketplace: fair trade, consumer protection, and the hisbah system.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: When Prophet Muhammad arrived in Medina in 622 CE, the marketplace was a place where the clever merchant won and ordinary people lost. He transformed it entirely by establishing open access, banning sham bidding and hoarding, and creating the hisbah system of market inspectors. Discover how 7th-century marketplace reforms created the foundation for Islamic commercial law.

linkedin.post: When Prophet Muhammad arrived in Medina in 622 CE, he found a marketplace where clever merchants prospered while ordinary people suffered. His response was revolutionary: comprehensive market reform. He established open access for all traders, banned sham bidding and hoarding, and created the hisbah system — appointed market inspectors who ensured fair dealing. These weren't just moral guidelines; they were enforceable regulations with real consequences. The marketplace transformation in 7th-century Medina laid the groundwork for Islamic commercial law and created principles we now recognize as fundamental to consumer protection. What strikes me most is how these reforms prioritized market access and transparency — concepts we're still working to perfect today. Listen to the full episode: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-2

short_video.title: The First Market Regulators Were in 7th Century Medina
short_video.hook: You think market regulation is modern? Think again.
short_video.voiceover: When Prophet Muhammad arrived in Medina in 622 CE, he found a marketplace where clever merchants won and ordinary people lost. His solution was revolutionary. He established the hisbah system — appointed market inspectors who banned sham bidding and hoarding. They ensured open access for all traders and fair dealing in every transaction. These weren't just moral guidelines. They were enforceable regulations with real consequences. The marketplace reforms in 7th-century Medina became the foundation for Islamic commercial law, creating consumer protection principles 1,400 years before we thought we invented them.
